title: White House Weighs In on Legislation to Close Cloud Loophole for AI Chip Exports
summary:
The White House has provided behind-the-scenes feedback on the MATCH Act and AI Overwatch, two export control bills currently under negotiation for the National Defense Authorization Act. The administration's engagement suggests it is open to collaborating on legislation to close regulatory loopholes that allow foreign entities to remotely access advanced artificial intelligence hardware through overseas cloud providers.

The move follows reports that Moonshot AI, the developer of the Kimi models, sought to rent more than 8,000 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs from European data centers to bypass U.S. shipping bans. To secure the capacity, Moonshot reportedly offered upfront payments 30% to 50% higher than those of non-Chinese customers. This coincides with plans by a new Democratic majority in Congress to call Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify on whether the company has done enough to prevent its chips from reaching U.S. adversaries.

CHINESE AI LAB SEEKS NVIDIA BLACKWELL CHIPS THROUGH EUROPEAN DATA CENTERS

China's Moonshot AI has reportedly explored renting Nvidia's advanced Blackwell computing capacity in Europe, potentially circumventing US restrictions on chip exports to China.

According to CNBC, discussions included access to clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs, with Moonshot potentially offering 30%–50% higher upfront payments than non-Chinese customers.

US export controls restrict physical chip shipments to China, but remote access through overseas cloud providers remains a regulatory gap.

Washington is considering legislation to close that loophole.

MOONSHOT SEEKS $NVDA BLACKWELL ACCESS IN EUROPE

Chinese AI lab Moonshot, the developer of Kimi, has held talks to rent clusters of 8,000+ Nvidia Blackwell GPUs from European 🇪🇺 neoclouds, primarily for inference and potentially training, CNBC reports.

The White House previously accused Moonshot of accessing Blackwell chips remotely through a data center in Thailand.

U.S. export controls restrict shipments of these chips to China, but don't broadly prohibit Chinese companies from renting the same computing power through overseas cloud providers.

One proposed arrangement reportedly involved Moonshot paying 30%-50% more upfront than non-Chinese customers, reflecting the risk of future restrictions.

No completed deal has been confirmed.
